explanation.en: In Spanish, age is expressed with tener. At A0, learn the pattern tengo ... años.
At A0, learn el/la as the and un/una as a or one with familiar nouns. Do not try to memorize all gender rules yet.
Qué, cómo, dónde, and quién are written with accents in direct questions. Spanish direct questions normally begin with ¿ and end with ?.
Use me llamo plus a name to say your name. Do not change the pattern when only the name changes.
Use soy de plus a city or country to say where you are from. Keep de in the pattern.
Before e or i, qu represents the k sound in words like queso. In gue and gui, the u keeps g hard in words such as Miguel.
Spanish spelling is often more regular than English. Vowels are stable, h is silent, ñ is its own letter, and written accents can mark stress or meaning.
A safe beginner pattern is subject plus verb plus complement. Spanish often omits yo when the verb already shows I.
Use tengo for I have, tienes for you have, and tiene for he, she, or a named person has.
Spanish has greetings that fit the time of day. The boundaries are flexible, so learn them as useful choices rather than exact clock rules.

examples.0.en: Me llamo Ana. = My name is Ana.

examples.1.en: Soy de Madrid. = I am from Madrid.

examples.2.en: Tengo un libro. = I have a book.

examples.3.en: Ana tiene un libro. = Ana has a book.

explanation.en: Very short Spanish sentences often use subject plus verb plus the rest of the idea. At A0, keep familiar patterns intact: Me llamo Ana, Soy de Madrid, Tengo un libro, and Ana tiene un libro. Do not rearrange the words randomly; Spanish word order can vary later, but these beginner patterns should be memorized as stable chunks.

title.en: Basic word order in short sentences

examples.0.en: Tengo un libro. = I have a book.

examples.2.en: Ana tiene un libro. = Ana has a book.

examples.4.en: Common mistake: Soy hambre. Use Tengo hambre.

explanation.en: Tener means to have. At A0, use tengo for I have, tienes for you have, and recognize tiene for he/she has. Pronunciation: tener = teh-NEHR, tengo = TEHN-goh, tienes = TYEH-nes, tiene = TYEH-neh. Use tener for possessions, as in Tengo un libro. Spanish also uses tener in fixed expressions such as Tengo hambre. A common beginner mistake is translating I am hungry with soy or estoy; for this expression, use tengo hambre.
In Spanish, the letter h is usually written but not pronounced. Read hola as ola and hambre as ambre. The spelling still keeps h.
Spanish vowels are stable in simple words. The vowel sound in hola, adiós, gracias, and por favor stays clear and short.
Use buenos días in the morning, buenas tardes in the afternoon, and buenas noches in the evening or at night. Hola works at any time.
Use me llamo plus a name to introduce yourself. Keep the pattern stable when the name changes.
Use ¿Cómo te llamas? to ask one person their name in a friendly introduction.

Spanish ñ, j and ll are important in names and first words. In this course, ll uses the same broad yeista pronunciation category as consonantal y. ll is two lowercase l letters: l + l. Do not confuse it with two uppercase I letters.

title.en: ñ, j and ll in names

explanation.en: Use soy de plus a place for a simple origin line in an introduction. Keep de in the pattern.
Use mucho gusto or encantado/encantada after meeting someone. Igualmente means likewise.
Use ¿De dónde eres? to ask one person where they are from. De dónde asks for origin, not current residence.
Use ¿Dónde vives? to ask where one person lives.

examples.0.en: Me llamo Marta. Soy de Ucrania. Vivo en Kyiv. Hablo ucraniano y ruso.

explanation.en: A tiny profile can combine name, origin, residence and languages with short sentences.
Use hablo plus a language to say what language you speak. Use hablas in the question to ask another person.
Use hablo un poco de plus a language for limited ability. Keep de before the language.

title.en: A little with un poco de

explanation.en: Soy de tells where someone is from. Vivo en tells where someone lives now. Do not swap the patterns when the prompt asks for one specific meaning.
Use soy de plus a country or city to say where you are from. Keep de in the pattern; it is part of the meaning.
In direct questions, qué and dónde are written with accents. Spanish direct questions also begin with ¿.
Use vivo en plus a place to say where you live. Use soy de for origin and vivo en for residence.
Some role and description words change final -o to -a for feminine forms. This module teaches only common pairs used in the lessons.
Use ¿Cómo es? to ask what a person is like. Answer with es plus one short description.

examples.1.en: Es mi amiga. Se llama Marta.

explanation.en: A short everyday conversation can identify a person, give a role, and add one origin, residence or language fact.
Use mi for my and tu for your. In this module, keep roles short: mi amigo, mi amiga, tu profesor.
Use se llama to say another person’s name. Use me llamo for yourself and te llamas when asking you.

examples.0.en: Soy de Ucrania. / Es de Ucrania.

examples.1.en: Vivo en Kyiv. / Vive en Kyiv.

explanation.en: Use es, vive and habla for another person. Contrast with soy/vivo/hablo for yourself and eres/vives/hablas for you.
Use ¿Quién es? to ask who a person is. Use es to identify another person. This is third-person use, not self-introduction.

examples.0.en: ¿Es tu amigo? Sí, es mi amigo.

explanation.en: Use ¿Es...? or ¿Habla...? to ask a yes/no question about another person. Answer sí or no without changing the facts.
Use caro or barato with practiced masculine objects. Use cara or barata with practiced feminine objects. Keep the object and adjective together: el libro es caro, la bolsa es barata.
At A0, use esto in the question ¿Qué es esto? Use este before a masculine noun and esta before a feminine noun when choosing an item: este libro, esta botella.

In the shop role-play, use the polite fixed question ¿Tiene...? to ask whether the seller has an item. The seller may answer Sí, tenemos... or No, no tenemos.... This module does not teach the full tú/usted contrast.
Use ¿Cuánto cuesta? to ask the price of one item. Answer with Cuesta... euros. For a simple total, Son... euros may also be used. The practiced prices are one, two, three, five and ten euros.

title.en: Asking and stating a simple price

explanation.en: Use Quiero... for a simple purchase intention and Este/Esta, por favor to point to one item. Use Nada más, gracias to answer ¿Algo más? when you do not want anything else.
Use ¿Qué es esto? to ask what an unknown object is. Answer with Es un... or Es una... The question asks for an object name, not a price.
Use un with practiced masculine objects such as libro and cuaderno. Use una with practiced feminine objects such as botella, bolsa and llave. This module teaches only these familiar examples.

title.en: un and una with familiar objects

explanation.en: Use ¿Cómo llego a...? to ask how to get somewhere. Use ¿Cómo voy a...? to ask how to travel there. These are route questions, not location answers.
Use está to say where a place is: La estación está cerca. Use es to identify what something is: Es un hotel. This module only contrasts these fixed uses.
Use cerca for near and lejos for far. With a place, use está: La farmacia está cerca.
Use the fixed directions Sigue recto, Gira a la izquierda and Gira a la derecha. In route-sequence tasks, order matters.
Use Voy en... for bus, train, metro, taxi, car and bicycle. Use Voy a pie for on foot. For advice, use Toma el metro or Ve en autobús as fixed A0 phrases.
Use ¿Dónde está...? to ask where a place is. The answer should locate the place, not give transport.
When you do not understand, say no entiendo. Then ask for one clear action: repita, por favor or hable más despacio, por favor. These are fixed polite requests in this module.
For urgent help, keep the sentence short and direct. Use necesito with médico or policía, or say es una emergencia. The app does not teach broad emergency conversation yet.
Necesito means I need. At A0, use it with one clear thing: necesito ayuda, necesito un médico, necesito la policía. Do not use it for long explanations yet.
Use a short polite word before asking for help. Disculpe is the safest general choice in this module. Oiga can attract attention, but keep it polite and follow with a clear request.
¿Puede ayudarme? is a polite fixed question meaning Can you help me? Use it when you need help from another person. It is a question, so it keeps Spanish question marks.
Use the known pattern ¿Dónde está...? to ask where an important place is. In this module, the places are el baño, la farmacia and el hospital.

title.en: Asking where an important service is

explanation.en: Use este with masculine nouns and esta with feminine nouns in controlled family sentences. Do not teach the full demonstrative system here; only produce useful sentences such as Este es mi padre and Esta es mi madre.

examples.0.en: Hay una mesa en la cocina.

examples.1.en: La mesa está en la cocina.

examples.2.en: Hay una cama en el dormitorio.

explanation.en: Use hay to say that something exists in a place. Use está to locate a specific known thing or person.
Use este/esta with rooms in fixed identification sentences. The focus is recognizing and naming rooms, not a complete gender lesson.

examples.0.en: La mesa está en la cocina.

examples.1.en: Mi madre está en el salón.

examples.2.en: La cama está en el dormitorio.

explanation.en: Use está to locate a known person or object. The known item comes first, then está en plus the room or place.
Use tengo to speak about yourself, tienes to ask another person, and tiene to speak about another person. Keep the pattern bounded to family facts.
Use se llama to state another person's name. In this module it combines with family words: Mi hermana se llama Marta.
Use quién to ask who a person is. Use dónde to ask where a person, room, or object is.
Estoy describes the speaker condition. Está can locate a known place or person. Do not use soy for temporary health condition.

title.en: Estoy for condition, está for location

explanation.en: Use estoy to say how you feel, estás to ask one person, and está to speak about another person. Keep this bounded to simple health or condition phrases.
Use short questions to check what is wrong. This module uses tú questions such as ¿Qué te pasa? and ¿Tienes fiebre?

examples.0.en: Disculpe. No estoy bien. Necesito una farmacia.

examples.1.en: ¿Qué te pasa? Me duele la cabeza.

explanation.en: A simple health exchange can combine attention, condition, symptom, service request, location and communication repair. Keep the sequence short and authored.
Use me duele plus one controlled body word to say where something hurts. Treat it as a fixed useful pattern at A0.
Use necesito with one clear health service or help word. The app teaches language for requesting help, not medical advice.
Use tengo fiebre for I have a fever. Use tienes fiebre to ask one person. This is a fixed beginner health pattern, not a full medical explanation.

examples.0.en: Me llamo Ana. = My name is Ana.

examples.1.en: Hola, me llamo Luis. = Hello, my name is Luis.

examples.2.en: ¿Cómo te llamas? = What is your name?

explanation.en: Use me llamo plus a name to say your name. Use ¿cómo te llamas? to ask one person their name in a friendly informal situation. At A0, learn these as practical introduction patterns.

examples.0.en: Soy de Madrid. = I am from Madrid.

examples.1.en: Soy de México. = I am from Mexico.

examples.2.en: ¿De dónde eres? = Where are you from?

explanation.en: Use soy de plus a place to say where you are from. Use ¿de dónde eres? to ask one person where they are from. At A0, learn these as practical first-contact patterns.

examples.0.en: Yo soy Ana. = I am Ana.

examples.1.en: Tú eres Luis. = You are Luis.

examples.2.en: Hola. Yo soy Ana. = Hello. I am Ana.

explanation.en: Spanish uses personal pronouns to show who is speaking or being addressed. In first-contact phrases, yo means I and tú means you. Spanish often omits pronouns because the verb form already shows the person, but beginners can use yo and tú to make meaning clear. Tú is informal singular you.

examples.1.en: Yo soy Ana. = I am Ana.

examples.2.en: Tú eres Luis. = You are Luis.

examples.3.en: Hola. Soy Ana. = Hello. I am Ana.

explanation.en: Ser means to be. In first introductions, use soy for I am and eres for you are. The useful beginner pattern is Yo soy + name and Tú eres + name. Do not use soy with tú, and do not use eres with yo.

title.en: Ser in the present: soy and eres

explanation.en: Use llamarse to say what someone is called.
